levels.confinement: Death or life without parole (life with parole if under 18 at the offense)

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Consent to Inspection
offenses.summary: Refuses to let the Texas Alcoholic Beverage Commission, its representative, or a peace officer enter a licensed or permitted premises for inspection.
offenses.heading: CONSENT TO INSPECTION; PENALTY

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Alcoholic Beverages in Dry Areas
offenses.summary: In a dry area, manufactures, sells, imports, transports, distributes, stores, takes orders for, or possesses with intent to sell an alcoholic beverage (unless otherwise allowed by the code).

tiers.when: Two or more prior convictions under this section

offenses.heading: ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES IN DRY AREAS

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Sale or Delivery to Certain Persons
offenses.summary: With criminal negligence sells an alcoholic beverage to a habitual drunkard or an intoxicated or insane person, or delivers one for commercial purposes to an intoxicated person.

tiers.level: Misdemeanor: fine $100 to $500 and/or up to 1 year jail
Misdemeanor: fine $500 to $1,000 and/or up to 1 year jail
tiers.when: Prior conviction under this section or for sale to a minor (106.03)

offenses.heading: SALE OR DELIVERY TO CERTAIN PERSONS

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Consignment Sale Prohibited
offenses.summary: Is a party to, or directly or indirectly interested in, a consignment sale of an alcoholic beverage.
offenses.notes: No penalty is stated in this section, so the Alcoholic Beverage Code general penalty (1.05) applies.

tiers.level: Misdemeanor: fine $100 to $1,000 and/or up to 1 year jail

offenses.heading: CONSIGNMENT SALE PROHIBITED

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Consumption of Alcoholic Beverage on Premises Licensed for Off-Premises Consumption
offenses.summary: Knowingly consumes liquor or beer on the premises of a business licensed only for off-premise sales (such as a convenience store). Knowledge is presumed if the required warning sign is posted.
offenses.heading: CONSUMPTION OF ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGE ON PREMISES LICENSED FOR OFF-PREMISES CONSUMPTION

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Consumption of Alcoholic Beverages Near Schools
offenses.summary: Possesses an open container or consumes an alcoholic beverage on a public street, alley, or sidewalk within 1,000 feet of the property line of a public or private school (pre-K through 12th grade).
offenses.heading: CONSUMPTION OF ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES NEAR SCHOOLS

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Unlawful Display or Use of Permit or License
offenses.summary: Knowingly lets another use a TABC permit or license in a way not allowed by law, or uses another's permit or license.
offenses.heading: UNLAWFUL DISPLAY OR USE OF PERMIT OR LICENSE

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.chapter: Ch. 105 Hours of Sale and Consumption
offenses.name: Hours of Sale: Beer and Malt Beverages
offenses.summary: Not a separate offense (selling outside these hours is an offense under 105.10). Beer may be sold 7 a.m. to midnight Monday through Saturday; on Sunday from midnight to 1 a.m. and noon to midnight. Exceptions: on-premise licensees may serve beer with food from 10 a.m. to noon on Sunday; retail dealers may sell for off-premise consumption from 10 a.m. to noon on Sunday; late-hours on-premise licensees may sell until 2 a.m. in large cities and counties and where locally adopted.
aliases: Hours of Sale of Beer Prohibited
offenses.heading: HOURS OF SALE: MALT BEVERAGES

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.chapter: Ch. 105 Hours of Sale and Consumption
offenses.name: Hours of Consumption
offenses.summary: Consumes or possesses with intent to consume an alcoholic beverage in a public place (including a bar or other licensed premises) during prohibited hours. Standard-hours areas: 12:15 a.m. to 7 a.m. (Sunday 1:15 a.m. to noon). Extended-hours areas: 2:15 a.m. to 7 a.m. (Sunday 2:15 a.m. to noon).
offenses.notes: Proof of possession with intent to consume requires evidence the person drank during the prohibited hours that day. Hotel guests may drink in the hotel bar at any time.
offenses.heading: HOURS OF CONSUMPTION

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.chapter: Ch. 105 Hours of Sale and Consumption
offenses.name: Sale or Consumption During Prohibited Hours (Licensee)
offenses.summary: In violation of the hours of sale, sells or offers to sell an alcoholic beverage during prohibited hours, or consumes or permits consumption on the person's licensed or permitted premises during prohibited hours.
aliases: Consume or Permits Alcoholic Beverage on Licensed Premises During Prohibited Hours
Sell Alcoholic Beverage during Prohibited Hours
offenses.heading: PENALTY

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Purchase of Alcohol by a Minor
offenses.summary: A minor (under 21) purchases an alcoholic beverage (except under the immediate supervision of a peace officer enforcing the code).
offenses.notes: A "minor" is anyone under 21. On conviction or deferred disposition the court orders 8-12 hours of alcohol-related community service (20-40 with one prior) and a driver's license suspension of 30 days (60 with one prior, 180 with two or more) (106.071(d)).

tiers.level: Fine $250 to $2,000 and/or up to 180 days jail
tiers.when: Minor who is not a "child" (17 or older) with two or more prior convictions

offenses.heading: PURCHASE OF ALCOHOL BY A MINOR

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Attempt to Purchase Alcohol by a Minor
offenses.summary: A minor (under 21), with specific intent to purchase alcohol, does an act amounting to more than mere preparation that tends but fails to complete the purchase.
offenses.notes: A "minor" is anyone under 21. On conviction or deferred disposition the court orders 8-12 hours of alcohol-related community service (20-40 with one prior) and a driver's license suspension of 30 days (60 with one prior, 180 with two or more) (106.071(d)).

tiers.level: Fine $250 to $2,000 and/or up to 180 days jail
tiers.when: Minor who is not a "child" (17 or older) with two or more prior convictions

offenses.heading: ATTEMPT TO PURCHASE ALCOHOL BY A MINOR

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Sale to Minors
offenses.summary: With criminal negligence sells an alcoholic beverage to a minor (under 21).
offenses.notes: No offense if the minor showed apparently valid government photo ID (driver's license, ID card, passport, or military ID) showing age 21 or older and matching the minor's appearance (subsection (b)).
offenses.heading: SALE TO MINORS

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Consumption of Alcohol by a Minor
offenses.summary: A minor (under 21) consumes an alcoholic beverage.
offenses.notes: Affirmative defense: consumed in the visible presence of the minor's adult parent, guardian, or spouse. Does not apply to a minor who was the first to call for emergency medical help for a possible alcohol overdose and stayed and cooperated (subsection (e)). A "minor" is anyone under 21. On conviction or deferred disposition the court orders 8-12 hours of alcohol-related community service (20-40 with one prior) and a driver's license suspension of 30 days (60 with one prior, 180 with two or more) (106.071(d)).

tiers.level: Fine $250 to $2,000 and/or up to 180 days jail
tiers.when: Minor who is not a "child" (17 or older) with two or more prior convictions

offenses.heading: CONSUMPTION OF ALCOHOL BY A MINOR

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Driving or Operating Watercraft under the Influence of Alcohol by Minor
offenses.summary: A minor (under 21) operates a motor vehicle in a public place, or a watercraft, with any detectable amount of alcohol in their system.
offenses.notes: If the minor was intoxicated (0.08 or loss of normal use), DWI (PC 49.04) may also apply. License suspension and alcohol education apply on conviction.

tiers.level: Fine $500 to $2,000 and/or up to 180 days jail
tiers.when: Minor 17 or older with two or more prior convictions under this section

offenses.heading: DRIVING OR OPERATING WATERCRAFT UNDER THE INFLUENCE OF ALCOHOL BY MINOR

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Possession of Alcohol by a Minor
offenses.summary: A minor (under 21) possesses an alcoholic beverage.
offenses.notes: Allowed: while working for a licensee in lawful employment; in the visible presence of an adult parent, guardian, spouse, or court-appointed custodian; under peace officer supervision for enforcement; or as lawfully provided under 106.16. Medical-amnesty exception as in 106.04. A "minor" is anyone under 21. On conviction or deferred disposition the court orders 8-12 hours of alcohol-related community service (20-40 with one prior) and a driver's license suspension of 30 days (60 with one prior, 180 with two or more) (106.071(d)).

tiers.level: Fine $250 to $2,000 and/or up to 180 days jail
tiers.when: Minor who is not a "child" (17 or older) with two or more prior convictions

offenses.heading: POSSESSION OF ALCOHOL BY A MINOR

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Purchase of Alcohol for a Minor; Furnishing Alcohol to a Minor
offenses.summary: Purchases an alcoholic beverage for, or gives one to, a minor (under 21).
offenses.notes: Allowed for the minor's adult parent, guardian, or spouse (or court-appointed custodian) who is visibly present when the minor drinks it.

tiers.when: The minor, as a result of drinking it, caused serious bodily injury or death to another person

offenses.heading: PURCHASE OF ALCOHOL FOR A MINOR; FURNISHING ALCOHOL TO A MINOR

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Misrepresentation of Age by a Minor
offenses.summary: A minor (under 21) falsely states they are 21 or older, or presents a document showing they are 21 or older, to a person selling or serving alcoholic beverages.
offenses.notes: Using a fake or altered driver's license may also be an offense under Transportation Code 521.451-.456. A "minor" is anyone under 21. On conviction or deferred disposition the court orders 8-12 hours of alcohol-related community service (20-40 with one prior) and a driver's license suspension of 30 days (60 with one prior, 180 with two or more) (106.071(d)).

tiers.level: Fine $250 to $2,000 and/or up to 180 days jail
tiers.when: Minor who is not a "child" (17 or older) with two or more prior convictions

offenses.heading: MISREPRESENTATION OF AGE BY A MINOR

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Punishment for Alcohol Offenses by Minors
offenses.summary: Not a separate offense. Sets the punishment for a minor's purchase, attempted purchase, consumption, possession, or misrepresentation of age: a Class C misdemeanor; or, for a minor 17 or older with two prior convictions, a fine of $250 to $2,000 and/or up to 180 days in jail (no deferred disposition). Also requires alcohol-related community service and a driver's license suspension (30, 60, or 180 days by number of priors). Juvenile adjudications and deferred dispositions count as prior convictions.
offenses.heading: PUNISHMENT FOR ALCOHOL-RELATED OFFENSE BY MINOR

offenses.group: Title 4. Regulatory and Penal Provisions
offenses.name: Prohibited Activities by Persons Younger than 18
offenses.summary: A TABC permittee or licensee employs, permits, or induces a person younger than 18 to dance with another person for a benefit on the licensed premises.
offenses.heading: PROHIBITED ACTIVITIES BY PERSONS YOUNGER THAN 18

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Searches and Seizures (Texas Guarantee)
offenses.summary: Not an offense. People are secure in their persons, houses, papers, and possessions from unreasonable searches and seizures. No warrant to search a place or seize a person or thing may issue without describing them as nearly as possible and without probable cause supported by oath or affirmation.
offenses.heading: SEARCHES AND SEIZURES

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Who Is a Peace Officer
offenses.summary: Not an offense. Lists who is a peace officer in Texas, including sheriffs and deputies, constables and deputies, municipal police officers and marshals, DPS officers and Rangers, district and county attorney investigators, TABC agents, arson investigators, school district and college police, Parks and Wildlife game wardens, and many other commissioned officers. Reserve officers are included only if they hold a permanent peace officer license.
offenses.warning: The Legislature passed two versions of this article in 2025; both appear in the statute text. Check which list applies.
offenses.heading: PEACE OFFICERS GENERALLY

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: General Duties of Peace Officers
offenses.summary: Not an offense. Every peace officer must: preserve the peace in their jurisdiction by all lawful means; interfere without a warrant to prevent or suppress crime where this Code allows; execute lawful process from a magistrate or court; notify a magistrate of offenses committed in their jurisdiction; and arrest offenders without a warrant when the law allows, so they can be taken before a magistrate.
offenses.heading: GENERAL POWERS AND DUTIES OF PEACE OFFICERS

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Summoning Aid
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An officer who meets resistance while performing a legal duty must summon enough county residents to overcome it, and a person summoned must obey. Under 2A.054, an officer whose summons is refused must report the person to the district or county attorney for prosecution.
offenses.heading: SUMMONING AID

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Child Safety Check Alert (TCIC)
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An officer who locates a child or other person on the TCIC child safety check alert list must immediately call DFPS on its law-enforcement intake line, ask DFPS about the case, and ask the child and the other person about the child's safety, well-being, and current residence. The officer may temporarily detain them to make sure the child is safe, may take possession of the child without a court order if Family Code 262.104 applies, and otherwise must get the current address and report it to DFPS, then report to TCIC that the person was located.
offenses.heading: RESPONSE TO CHILD SAFETY CHECK ALERT

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Releasing a Child Taken Into Possession
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A child taken under Family Code 262.104 may be released to a licensed and authorized child-care facility, juvenile probation, DFPS, or another person authorized by law. Before releasing a child to a non-government person, the officer must check NCIC that the child is not missing, check NCIC for protective orders, warrants, sex offender registration, and supervised release on that person, call the DFPS abuse hotline to check the abuse registry, and complete the other checks the article lists.
offenses.heading: RELEASE OF CHILD BY LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICER

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Stalking, Harassment, or Terroristic Threat Investigations
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An officer investigating stalking (PC 42.072), harassment (PC 42.07), or a terroristic threat (PC 22.07) must advise any possible adult victim of all reasonable means to prevent further offenses, including giving them the written notice adopted by the Health and Human Services Commission. The officer may also give local victim resource information.
offenses.heading: DUTIES OF PEACE OFFICER INVESTIGATING STALKING, HARASSMENT, OR TERRORISTIC THREAT

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Asking Victims or Witnesses About Immigration Status
offenses.summary: Not an offense. While investigating an offense, an officer may ask about a victim's or witness's nationality or immigration status only if needed to investigate the offense or to tell them about federal visas for people who help law enforcement. This does not stop the officer from investigating another offense, or from asking if there is probable cause the victim or witness committed a separate offense.
offenses.heading: NATIONALITY OR IMMIGRATION STATUS INQUIRY

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Misused Identity Notification
offenses.summary: Not an offense. When an arrested person gave someone else's identifying information as their own, the agency that collects arrestee identifying information in that county must notify the victim (including that they may file a DPS declaration and are entitled to expunction) and notify DPS of the misuse and, if known, the arrestee's actual identity.
offenses.heading: MISUSED IDENTITY NOTIFICATIONS

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 2B Law Enforcement Interactions with Public
offenses.name: Racial Profiling: Definitions
offenses.summary: Not an offense. "Racial profiling" is a law-enforcement-initiated action based on a person's race, ethnicity, or national origin rather than on their behavior or on information identifying them as having engaged in criminal activity. A "motor vehicle stop" is any stop of a motor vehicle for an alleged violation of a law or ordinance. Race or ethnicity categories for reports are: Alaska Native or American Indian; Asian or Pacific Islander; Black; Hispanic or Latino; and White.
offenses.heading: DEFINITIONS

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 2B Law Enforcement Interactions with Public
offenses.name: Racial Profiling Prohibited
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A peace officer may not engage in racial profiling. Each agency must have a written racial profiling policy, a complaint process, and must take corrective action against officers found to have engaged in it (2B.0053).
offenses.heading: RACIAL PROFILING PROHIBITED

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 2B Law Enforcement Interactions with Public
offenses.name: Motor Vehicle Stop Reports
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An officer who makes a motor vehicle stop must report to their agency: the detained driver's gender and race or ethnicity (as the driver states it, or as the officer determines to the best of their ability); the initial reason for the stop; whether a search was made, whether it was by consent, the reason (plain view, probable cause or reasonable suspicion, tow inventory, or arrest), and what was found; whether an arrest was made and whether it was for a Penal Code offense, a traffic violation, or a warrant, and the charge; the location; whether a warning or citation was issued; and whether the officer used physical force that caused bodily injury.
offenses.heading: REPORTS REQUIRED FOR MOTOR VEHICLE STOPS

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 2B Law Enforcement Interactions with Public
offenses.name: Body Worn Camera: When to Record
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An officer with a body worn camera must follow their agency's policy on when it must be activated. The officer may choose not to record, or stop recording, an encounter that is not related to an investigation. An officer who does not activate the camera on a call for assistance must note the reason in the incident report or case file. A claim that activating was unsafe, unrealistic, or impracticable is judged by what a reasonable officer would have done in the same situation.
offenses.heading: RECORDING INTERACTIONS WITH PUBLIC

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 2B Law Enforcement Interactions with Public
offenses.name: Unauthorized Release of Body Worn Camera Recording
offenses.summary: A peace officer or other law enforcement agency employee releases a body worn camera recording without the agency's permission.
offenses.heading: OFFENSE

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 2B Law Enforcement Interactions with Public
offenses.name: DWI Stop and Arrest Video: Defendant's Right to a Copy
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A person stopped or arrested on suspicion of DWI (PC 49.04), DWI with a child passenger (49.045), intoxication assault (49.07), or intoxication manslaughter (49.08) is entitled to a copy of any video made by or at the direction of the officer showing the stop, the arrest, their conduct during the encounter including field sobriety tests, or the breath or blood specimen being taken.
offenses.heading: VIDEO RECORDINGS OF ARRESTS FOR INTOXICATION OFFENSES

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 2B Law Enforcement Interactions with Public
offenses.name: Recording Custodial Interrogations (Serious Felonies)
offenses.summary: Not an offense. Unless good cause makes it infeasible, an agency must make a complete electronic recording of any custodial interrogation in a place of detention of a person suspected of or charged with murder, capital murder, kidnapping, aggravated kidnapping, trafficking of persons, continuous trafficking, continuous sexual abuse of a young child, indecency with a child, improper educator-student relationship, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, or sexual performance by a child. The recording must start when the person enters the interrogation area or receives the 38.22 warnings, whichever is earlier, and run until the interrogation ends.
offenses.heading: RECORDING OF CUSTODIAL INTERROGATION REQUIRED; EXCEPTIONS

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 2B Law Enforcement Interactions with Public
offenses.name: Duty to Intervene and Report Excessive Force
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A peace officer must intervene to stop or prevent another officer from using force on a suspect when the force exceeds what is reasonable and the officer knows or should know that it violates state or federal law, puts a person at risk of bodily injury without being immediately necessary to avoid imminent bodily injury to an officer or another person, and is not required to apprehend the suspect. An officer who witnesses excessive force by another officer must promptly make a detailed report to their own supervisor.
offenses.heading: INTERVENTION REQUIRED FOR EXCESSIVE FORCE; REPORT REQUIRED

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 2B Law Enforcement Interactions with Public
offenses.name: Neck Restraints (Choke Holds) Prohibited
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A peace officer may not intentionally use a choke hold, carotid artery hold, or similar neck restraint in searching or arresting a person unless it is necessary to prevent serious bodily injury to or the death of the officer or another person.
offenses.heading: USE OF NECK RESTRAINTS DURING SEARCH OR ARREST PROHIBITED

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 2B Law Enforcement Interactions with Public
offenses.name: Duty to Request and Render Aid
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An officer who encounters an injured person while on duty must immediately, as necessary, request EMS and give first aid to the extent of their skill and training until EMS arrives. This does not apply if doing so would expose the officer or another person to a risk of bodily injury, or if the officer is injured and physically unable.
offenses.heading: DUTY TO REQUEST AND RENDER AID

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Family Violence Calls: Officer Duties
offenses.summary: Not an offense. On a family violence call, the officer's primary duties are to protect any potential victim, enforce the law, enforce out-of-state protective orders, and make lawful arrests. The officer must check whether the address matches a licensed or verified foster home listed in TCIC, and must advise any possible adult victim of all reasonable means to prevent further family violence, including giving them the written notice adopted by the Health and Human Services Commission.
offenses.heading: DUTIES OF PEACE OFFICERS

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Family Violence Standby Assistance
offenses.summary: Not an offense. At the officer's discretion, the officer may stay with a family violence victim so the victim can safely remove their own or a child's personal property. The officer is not civilly liable for providing (or deciding whether to provide) the standby, and is not civilly or criminally liable if the victim wrongfully takes property.
offenses.heading: STANDBY ASSISTANCE; LIABILITY

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.chapter: Ch. 6 Preventing Offenses by the Act of Magistrates and Other Officers; Education Concerning Consequences of Certain Offenses
offenses.name: Duty to Prevent Offenses in View
offenses.summary: Not an offense. When a person is about to commit an offense against another person or their property, or to injure themself, in an officer's presence or view, the officer must prevent it and may summon citizens to help. The officer must use the force necessary to prevent the offense, and no greater. Under 6.05, an officer told of a threat to injure a person or property must prevent the threatened injury if within their power.
offenses.heading: PEACE OFFICER TO PREVENT INJURY

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Warrantless Arrest: Offense Within View
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A peace officer may arrest without a warrant for any offense committed in the officer's presence or view. Any person (including a private citizen) may arrest without a warrant for a felony or an offense against the public peace committed in their presence or view.
offenses.heading: OFFENSE WITHIN VIEW

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Within View of Magistrate
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A peace officer may arrest without a warrant when a felony or breach of the peace is committed in the presence or view of a magistrate who verbally orders the arrest.
offenses.heading: WITHIN VIEW OF MAGISTRATE

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Warrantless Arrest: Authority of Peace Officers
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A peace officer may arrest without a warrant: persons found in suspicious places under circumstances reasonably showing they committed a felony, a Penal Code Chapter 42 offense (disorderly conduct and related), breach of the peace, or public intoxication, or are about to commit an offense; a person who committed an assault causing bodily injury when there is danger of further injury; a person who violated a protective order (25.07) outside the officer's presence; a person who committed family violence; a person who interfered with an emergency call outside the officer's presence; a person whose admissible statement establishes probable cause of a felony; and a civilly committed sex offender who committed a felony. The officer MUST arrest for a protective order violation committed in their presence, and must stay at a family violence or protective order scene if reasonably necessary to verify it and prevent further violence. Outside their jurisdiction, licensed officers may arrest for offenses in their view (with limits on traffic offenses) and must notify the local agency.
offenses.heading: AUTHORITY OF PEACE OFFICERS

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Public Intoxication: Release in Lieu of Arrest
offenses.summary: Not an offense. Instead of arresting an adult for public intoxication, an officer may release them if detention is unnecessary for anyone's protection and the person is released to a responsible adult, or verbally consents to admission to a licensed substance use treatment program or a sobering facility that admits them. The officer and agency are not liable for damage caused by a person released this way.
offenses.heading: PUBLIC INTOXICATION

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Release in Lieu of Arrest: Intellectual or Developmental Disability
offenses.summary: Not an offense. For a person with an intellectual or developmental disability who lives in a waiver-program group home or ICF/IID, the officer may release the person at their residence instead of arresting them if jail is unnecessary to protect the person and the other residents, and the officer made reasonable efforts to consult the staff and the person. The officer and agency are not liable for damage caused by a person released this way.
offenses.heading: AUTHORITY TO RELEASE IN LIEU OF ARREST CERTAIN PERSONS WITH INTELLECTUAL OR DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITY

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: When Felony Has Been Committed
offenses.summary: Not an offense. When a credible person gives an officer satisfactory proof that a felony was committed and the offender is about to escape so there is no time to get a warrant, the officer may pursue and arrest without a warrant.
offenses.heading: WHEN FELONY HAS BEEN COMMITTED

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Warrantless Arrest: Entering a Residence
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An officer making a lawful warrantless arrest may use the same measures as under a warrant, but may not enter a residence to make the arrest unless a resident consents or exigent circumstances require it.
offenses.heading: RIGHTS OF OFFICER

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Arrest by Out-of-State Officer in Fresh Pursuit
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An officer of another state who is authorized to make felony arrests and is in fresh pursuit (pursuit without unreasonable delay) of a person reasonably suspected of a felony may continue the pursuit into Texas and arrest the person.
offenses.heading: ARREST BY PEACE OFFICER FROM OTHER JURISDICTION

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Taking Arrestee Before Magistrate; Cite and Release
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An arrested person must be taken before a magistrate without unnecessary delay and within 48 hours. For a Class C misdemeanor (other than public intoxication), the officer may issue a citation instead. For a Class A or B misdemeanor, if the person lives in the county, the officer may issue a citation instead of arresting only for: possession of marihuana or synthetic cannabinoids up to 4 ounces; criminal mischief or graffiti at the listed lower levels; theft or theft of service of $100 to $750; tampering with a temporary vehicle tag; Class B contraband in a correctional facility; and driving while license invalid. Citations must include the family-violence firearm warning.
offenses.heading: MUST TAKE OFFENDER BEFORE MAGISTRATE

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Arrest Warrant: Definition and Requirements
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An arrest warrant is a written order from a magistrate commanding a peace officer to take the accused into custody. Under 15.02 it must name the person (or describe them reasonably if the name is unknown), state the offense, and be signed by the magistrate with their office named. Under 15.06 a warrant from a clerk or magistrate (other than a mayor) may be executed by the officer anywhere in Texas.
offenses.heading: WARRANT OF ARREST

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Taking Arrestee Before Magistrate (Magistrate Warnings)
offenses.summary: Not an offense. The arresting or custodial officer must take the arrested person before a magistrate without unnecessary delay and no later than 48 hours after arrest (in person or by videoconference, in the county of arrest or another county). The magistrate warns the person of the accusation, the right to retain counsel, to remain silent, to have an attorney during any interview, to end the interview at any time, and to an examining trial, and of how to request appointed counsel, then sets bail if allowed. For an arrest under 17.292(a) (family violence, trafficking, sexual assault, stalking), the officer must give the magistrate the information needed for an order for emergency protection.
offenses.heading: DUTIES OF ARRESTING OFFICER AND MAGISTRATE

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: When a Person Is Arrested
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A person is arrested when actually placed under restraint or taken into custody by an officer or person executing an arrest warrant or arresting without a warrant. Under 15.23, an arrest may be made on any day and at any time of day or night.
offenses.heading: WHEN A PERSON IS ARRESTED

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Force in Making an Arrest
offenses.summary: Not an offense. All reasonable means may be used to make an arrest, but no greater force than necessary to secure the arrest and detention of the accused. See also Penal Code 9.51.
offenses.heading: WHAT FORCE MAY BE USED

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Breaking a Door to Arrest (Felony)
offenses.summary: Not an offense. For a felony, an officer may break down the door of a house to make an arrest if refused admittance after giving notice of their authority and purpose.
offenses.heading: MAY BREAK DOOR

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Making Authority Known; Warrant Not in Hand
offenses.summary: Not an offense. When executing an arrest warrant, the officer must tell the accused under what authority the arrest is made. The officer does not need the warrant in hand, but must show it as soon as possible on request, and if it is not in hand must tell the person the offense charged and that a warrant was issued. The warrant and its affidavit become public information once executed.
offenses.heading: AUTHORITY TO ARREST MUST BE MADE KNOWN

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: School Notification of Student Arrests
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An agency that arrests, or refers to juvenile authorities, a person it believes is a public school student, for an offense listed in Subsection (h), must try to determine whether they are enrolled and orally notify the school superintendent or designee within 24 hours or before the next school day, whichever is earlier, followed by written notice within seven days.
offenses.heading: NOTIFICATION TO SCHOOLS REQUIRED

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Magistrate's Order for Emergency Protection (MOEP)
offenses.summary: Not an offense (violation is PC 25.07). At the arrestee's magistrate appearance for family violence, trafficking (20A.02, 20A.03), sexual assault and indecent assault (22.011, 22.012, 22.021), or stalking (42.072), the magistrate may issue an emergency protective order on their own motion or at the request of the victim, the victim's guardian, a peace officer, or the prosecutor. It is mandatory for family violence involving serious bodily injury or use or exhibition of a deadly weapon. It may prohibit further violence, threatening or (for good cause) any contact, going near the victim's home, work, or child's school or child care, possessing a firearm (except certain on-duty peace officers), and tracking the victim. The victim need not be present. An order lasts 61 to 91 days, or 91 to 121 days when a deadly weapon was used or exhibited. The arresting or custodial officer must give the magistrate the information needed to issue it.
offenses.heading: MAGISTRATE'S ORDER FOR EMERGENCY PROTECTION

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Search Warrant: Probable Cause Affidavit
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A search warrant is a written magistrate's order directing a peace officer to search for and seize property (or photograph a child). No search warrant may issue unless a sworn affidavit sets out substantial facts establishing probable cause. The magistrate may consider information by telephone or other reliable electronic means, with the applicant under oath and the testimony recorded. The affidavit becomes public once the warrant is executed.
offenses.heading: SEARCH WARRANT

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Search Warrant: What May Be Seized
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A search warrant may issue for: stolen or unlawfully acquired property; property designed or used to commit an offense; weapons prohibited by the Penal Code; gambling devices; drugs, controlled substances, precursors, and paraphernalia; property whose possession is prohibited; implements of a crime; evidence of an offense or that a particular person committed it (not the accused's personal writings), which is the basis for blood warrants; persons; contraband subject to forfeiture; electronic customer data; and cell phones under 18.0215.
offenses.heading: GROUNDS FOR ISSUANCE

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Searching a Cell Phone
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An officer may not search a person's cell phone or other wireless device incident to arrest without a warrant from a judge. Without a warrant, an officer may search only if the owner or possessor consents, the device is reported stolen by its owner or possessor, or the officer reasonably believes it is possessed by a fugitive with a felony arrest warrant or that there is an immediate life-threatening situation. After an emergency or fugitive search, the officer must apply for a warrant as soon as practicable; if the judge finds the situation did not exist, the evidence is not admissible.
offenses.heading: ACCESS TO CELLULAR TELEPHONE OR OTHER WIRELESS COMMUNICATIONS DEVICE

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Executing a Search Warrant; Inventory
offenses.summary: Not an offense. The officer must execute a search warrant without delay and return it to the magistrate. The officer gives a copy of the warrant to the owner, or to the person in possession of the place if the owner is absent. Before taking property, the officer prepares a signed written inventory and gives a copy to the owner or person in possession, or leaves the warrant and inventory at the place if no one is present.
offenses.heading: EXECUTION OF WARRANTS

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Blood Warrant: Executing in an Adjacent County
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A search warrant to collect a blood specimen from a person suspected of an intoxication offense (PC 49.04, 49.045, 49.05, 49.06, 49.061, 49.065, 49.07, or 49.08) may be executed by any peace officer in any county adjacent to the county where it was issued.
offenses.heading: EXECUTION OF WARRANT FOR BLOOD SPECIMEN IN INTOXICATION OFFENSE

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Time Limit to Execute a Search Warrant
offenses.summary: Not an offense. Unless the magistrate sets a shorter time, a search warrant must be executed within three whole days, not counting the day issued or the day executed (15 days for a DNA specimen warrant; 10 days for certain electronic-data warrants). A warrant to search a phone or other storage device counts as executed on time if the device was seized in time; the data may be analyzed afterward.
offenses.heading: DAYS ALLOWED FOR WARRANT TO RUN

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Body Cavity Search During a Traffic Stop
offenses.summary: Not an offense. An officer may not conduct a body cavity search (inspection of the anal or vaginal cavity, not a pat-down) during a traffic stop without first obtaining a search warrant authorizing it.
offenses.heading: BODY CAVITY SEARCH DURING TRAFFIC STOP

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Photo and Live Lineup Procedures
offenses.summary: Not an offense. Each agency whose officers conduct photo or live lineups must adopt a written policy, either the model policy from the Bill Blackwood Law Enforcement Management Institute or its own policy meeting the same minimum evidence-based standards (filler selection, instructions to the witness, documenting the witness's confidence, blind or blinded administration, and so on).
offenses.heading: PHOTOGRAPH AND LIVE LINEUP IDENTIFICATION PROCEDURES

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Statements of the Accused (Texas Miranda Warnings)
offenses.summary: Not an offense. A statement from custodial interrogation is admissible only if, before the statement, the accused received the 15.17 magistrate warnings or these warnings: (1) the right to remain silent and that any statement may be used against them at trial; (2) any statement may be used as evidence in court; (3) the right to a lawyer before and during questioning; (4) the right to an appointed lawyer if they cannot afford one; and (5) the right to terminate the interview at any time. The accused must knowingly, intelligently, and voluntarily waive those rights. A written statement must show the warnings and waiver on its face. An oral statement must be electronically recorded, with the warnings and waiver on the recording, all voices identified, and the recording unaltered. An oral statement that leads to facts found to be true (such as hidden property or the weapon) can still be used.
offenses.notes: The fifth warning (right to terminate the interview) is a Texas requirement beyond federal Miranda. Non-custodial and volunteered statements are not covered by this article (Sec. 5).
offenses.heading: WHEN STATEMENTS MAY BE USED

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Texas Exclusionary Rule
offenses.summary: Not an offense. Evidence obtained by an officer or other person in violation of the Texas or U.S. Constitution or laws may not be used against the accused at trial, and when the evidence raises the issue the jury is told to disregard evidence it believes (or has a reasonable doubt) was illegally obtained. Exception: evidence obtained by an officer acting in objective good faith reliance on a warrant issued by a neutral magistrate based on probable cause.
offenses.notes: Broader than the federal rule: it covers violations of any Texas law, and evidence obtained by private persons, and has only the warrant-based good faith exception.
offenses.heading: EVIDENCE NOT TO BE USED

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Hate Crime Finding (Bias or Prejudice)
offenses.summary: Not an offense. In a trial for an offense against the person (Penal Code Title 5) or arson (28.02), criminal mischief (28.03), graffiti (28.08), or 42.0601, the judge must enter an affirmative finding if the trier of fact finds the defendant intentionally selected the victim or property because of bias or prejudice against a group identified by race, color, disability, religion, national origin or ancestry, age, gender, or sexual preference, or by status as a peace officer or judge. The finding raises punishment under PC 12.47. Document the facts showing bias in the report.
offenses.heading: FINDING THAT OFFENSE WAS COMMITTED BECAUSE OF BIAS OR PREJUDICE

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Seizing Contraband for Forfeiture
offenses.summary: Not an offense. Property subject to forfeiture may be seized with a search warrant, or without one if the owner or person in charge knowingly consents, it is incident to a consent search, it was already subject to a forfeiture judgment, or it is incident to a lawful arrest or search. The seizing officer has custody, must give the prosecutor a sworn statement listing the property and the reasons for seizure, and within 72 hours must seal it, move it where the court orders, or turn it over to a law enforcement agency (digital currency goes to an offline agency wallet).
offenses.heading: SEIZURE OF CONTRABAND

offenses.group: Title 1. Code of Criminal Procedure
offenses.name: Failure to Comply With Sex Offender Registration
offenses.summary: A person required to register as a sex offender fails to comply with any requirement of Chapter 62 (initial registration, verification, reporting a change of address, job, school, vehicle, or online identifiers, etc.).

tiers.when: Duty to register expires 10 years after release or discharge (62.101(b) or (c))
Lifetime registrant who verifies once a year
Lifetime registrant who must verify every 90 days
Prior conviction for failure to register
Used another person's identifying information (PC 32.51) during the offense

offenses.heading: FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH REGISTRATION REQUIREMENTS

offenses.group: Subtitle E. Protection of the Child
offenses.chapter: Ch. 261 Investigation of Report of Child Abuse or Neglect
offenses.name: Duty to Report Child Abuse or Neglect
offenses.summary: Not itself the offense (see 261.109). Anyone with reasonable cause to believe a child's physical or mental health or welfare has been harmed by abuse or neglect by any person must immediately make a report as the Family Code provides. A "professional" (a licensed or certified person, or state-licensed facility employee, who has direct contact with children through their work, such as teachers, nurses, doctors, day-care workers, and juvenile probation and detention officers) must report within 24 hours of first having reasonable cause to believe a child has been or may be abused or neglected or is a victim of indecency with a child, and may not delegate the report to someone else.
offenses.heading: PERSONS REQUIRED TO REPORT; TIME TO REPORT

offenses.group: Subtitle E. Protection of the Child
offenses.chapter: Ch. 261 Investigation of Report of Child Abuse or Neglect
offenses.name: False Report; Criminal Penalty; Civil Penalty
offenses.summary: With intent to deceive, knowingly makes a false report of child abuse or neglect.
offenses.notes: The court must order the person to pay the falsely accused person's attorney's fees and costs; a $1,000 civil penalty also applies.
offenses.heading: FALSE REPORT; CRIMINAL PENALTY; CIVIL PENALTY

offenses.group: Subtitle E. Protection of the Child
offenses.chapter: Ch. 261 Investigation of Report of Child Abuse or Neglect
offenses.name: Failure to Report Child Abuse or Neglect
offenses.summary: A person required to report suspected child abuse or neglect (261.101(a)), or a professional required to report (261.101(b)), knowingly fails to report as required.

tiers.when: Any person who fails to report (a)
Child had an intellectual disability, lived in a state supported living center or licensed ICF-IID facility, and the actor knew the child suffered serious bodily injury
Professional who intended to conceal the abuse or neglect

offenses.heading: FAILURE TO REPORT; PENALTY

offenses.group: Subtitle H. Public Health Provisions
offenses.name: Sale of Cigarettes, E-Cigarettes, or Tobacco Products to Persons Younger than 21 Years of Age Prohibited; Proof of Age Required
offenses.summary: With criminal negligence sells or gives a cigarette, e-cigarette (vape), or tobacco product to someone younger than 21, or to someone who intends to give it to a person under 21. A store employee who makes the sale is criminally responsible.
offenses.notes: Defense: the buyer showed apparently valid government photo ID showing age 21 or older. Exception: buyer 18 or older with a valid military ID.
offenses.heading: SALE OF CIGARETTES, E-CIGARETTES, OR TOBACCO PRODUCTS TO PERSONS YOUNGER THAN 21 YEARS OF AGE PROHIBITED; PROOF OF AGE REQUIRED

offenses.group: Subtitle H. Public Health Provisions
offenses.name: Possession, Purchase, Consumption, or Receipt of Cigarettes, E-Cigarettes, or Tobacco Products by Minors Prohibited
offenses.summary: A person younger than 21 possesses, purchases, consumes, or accepts a cigarette, e-cigarette (vape), or tobacco product, or shows false proof of age to get one.
offenses.notes: Exceptions: possession required by an employer for work, a compliance test, or a person 18 or older with a valid military ID. Since 2025 (S.B. 2024), "e-cigarette" includes any vaping device or liquid whether or not it contains nicotine (161.081).
offenses.heading: POSSESSION, PURCHASE, CONSUMPTION, OR RECEIPT OF CIGARETTES, E-CIGARETTES, OR TOBACCO PRODUCTS BY MINORS PROHIBITED

offenses.group: Subtitle B. Solid Waste, Toxic Chemicals, Sewage, Litter, and Water
offenses.name: Illegal Dumping; Discarding Lighted Materials
offenses.summary: Disposes of (or allows disposal of) litter or other solid waste anywhere other than an approved site, including within 300 feet of a public highway, on a right-of-way, on public or private property, in a dumpster without authorization, or into state waters; or receives or transports waste for disposal at an unapproved site. Subsection (a-1) covers throwing lighted litter (cigarette, match) that starts a fire.
offenses.notes: No culpable mental state is required except for the state jail felony tiers (subsection (n)). A repeat conviction can lead to forfeiture of the vehicle used.

tiers.when: 5 pounds or less, or 5 gallons or less
More than 5 pounds but less than 500 pounds, or more than 5 gallons but less than 100 cubic feet
500 pounds to less than 1,000 pounds, or 100 to less than 200 cubic feet
For a commercial purpose, more than 5 pounds but less than 200 pounds
1,000 pounds or more, or 200 cubic feet or more
For a commercial purpose, 200 pounds or more
Waste is in a closed barrel or drum

tiers.level: Misdemeanor: fine up to $500 and/or up to 30 days jail
tiers.when: Lighted litter that starts a fire (a-1), less than 500 pounds

offenses.heading: ILLEGAL DUMPING; DISCARDING LIGHTED MATERIALS; CRIMINAL PENALTIES

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Criminal Offenses Related to Prescription Information
offenses.summary: A person authorized to receive prescription monitoring program information discloses or uses it in an unauthorized way (a), or a person requesting it makes a material misrepresentation or omission (b).
offenses.heading: CRIMINAL OFFENSES RELATED TO PRESCRIPTION INFORMATION

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Penalty Groups (Quick Reference)
offenses.summary: Controlled substances are divided into penalty groups that set the punishment. Common examples, as listed in the statute: PG 1 (481.102): cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine, oxycodone, hydrocodone (most forms), morphine, hydromorphone, PCP, GHB, ketamine, flunitrazepam (Rohypnol). PG 1-A (481.1021): LSD (counted in abuse units). PG 1-B (481.1022): fentanyl and its analogues. PG 2 (481.103): MDMA (ecstasy), psilocybin and psilocin (mushrooms), mescaline, amphetamine, THC other than marihuana (wax, oils, concentrates). PG 2-A (481.1031): synthetic cannabinoids (K2, spice). PG 3 (481.104): benzodiazepines such as alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam, and clonazepam; carisoprodol; tramadol; zolpidem; methylphenidate; anabolic steroids; limited-strength hydrocodone or codeine combinations. PG 4 (481.105): low-strength codeine preparations (cough syrup) and buprenorphine. Marihuana has its own offenses (481.120, 481.121).
offenses.notes: Always check the full penalty group list for the specific substance. Hemp (delta-9 THC of 0.3% or less) is excluded from the definition of marihuana.
offenses.heading: CRIMINAL CLASSIFICATION

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Manufacture or Delivery of Substance in Penalty Group 1
offenses.summary: Knowingly manufactures, delivers, or possesses with intent to deliver a Penalty Group 1 substance (such as cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, or oxycodone).
offenses.notes: Drug-free zone (481.134): within 1,000 feet of a school, youth center, or playground, or on a school bus, can raise the level. Using a child to commit the offense (481.140) or a resulting death or serious bodily injury (481.141) raises it one degree.

Manufacture or Delivery of  Substance in PG1 (1g-4g)

Manufacture or Delivery of Substance in PG1 (4g-200g)

15 to 99 years or life; fine up to $250,000

20 to 99 years or life; fine up to $500,000

offenses.summary: Knowingly or intentionally delivers marihuana (including giving it away).
offenses.notes: Drug-free zone (481.134): within 1,000 feet of a school, youth center, or playground, or on a school bus, can raise the level.

tiers.extra: 10 to 99 years or life; fine up to $100,000

offenses.heading: OFFENSE: DELIVERY OF MARIHUANA

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Possession of Marihuana
offenses.summary: Knowingly or intentionally possesses a usable quantity of marihuana (the plant; THC concentrates such as wax and vape oil are Penalty Group 2, not marihuana).
offenses.notes: Hemp (delta-9 THC of 0.3% or less) is excluded from "marihuana". In a drug-free zone, 2 ounces or less becomes Class A (481.134(f)).

tiers.extra: 5 to 99 years or life; fine up to $50,000

offenses.heading: OFFENSE: POSSESSION OF MARIHUANA

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Delivery of Controlled Substance or Marihuana to Child
offenses.summary: Knowingly delivers a Penalty Group 1, 1-A, 1-B, 2, or 3 substance, or marihuana, to a child, to a student enrolled in a primary or secondary school, or to someone the actor believes will deliver it to a child or student.
offenses.heading: OFFENSE: DELIVERY OF CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE OR MARIHUANA TO CHILD

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Possession or Transport of Certain Chemicals with Intent to Manufacture Controlled Substance

Possession or Transport of Certain Chemicals with Intent to Manufacture Controlled Substance (PG1/1-A/1-B)
Possession or Transport of Certain Chemicals with Intent to Manufacture Controlled Substance (PG2)
Possession or Transport of Certain Chemicals with Intent to Manufacture Controlled Substance (PG3/4)

Scheduled substance not in any penalty group

offenses.heading: OFFENSE: POSSESSION OR TRANSPORT OF CERTAIN CHEMICALS WITH INTENT TO MANUFACTURE CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Possession or Transport of Anhydrous Ammonia; Use of or Tampering with Equipment

offenses.heading: OFFENSE: POSSESSION OR TRANSPORT OF ANHYDROUS AMMONIA; USE OF OR TAMPERING WITH EQUIPMENT

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Possession or Delivery of Drug Paraphernalia
offenses.summary: Knowingly or intentionally uses or possesses with intent to use drug paraphernalia to grow, make, prepare, package, store, or conceal a controlled substance, or to introduce one into the body (a); delivers or makes paraphernalia knowing it will be used that way (b); or an adult delivers it to someone under 18 and at least three years younger (c).
aliases: Possession or Delivery of Drug Paraphernalia (Delivery)
Possession or Delivery of Drug Paraphernalia (Minor)
Possession or Delivery of Drug Paraphernalia (Possession)

offenses.heading: OFFENSE: POSSESSION OR DELIVERY OF DRUG PARAPHERNALIA

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Illegal Barter, Expenditure, or Investment

tiers.when: Proceeds of, or financing, a life-punishable drug felony ((a)(1), (3))
Proceeds of, or financing, a 50 to 2,000 pound marihuana possession offense ((a)(2), (4))

offenses.heading: OFFENSE: ILLEGAL BARTER, EXPENDITURE, OR INVESTMENT

offenses.heading: OFFENSE AND CIVIL PENALTY: COMMERCIAL MATTERS

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Diversion of Controlled Substance by Registrants, Dispensers, and Certain Other Persons
offenses.summary: Knowingly converts to the person's own use (b)(1), or diverts to another's unlawful use (b)(2), a controlled substance the person has access to through their profession or employment.
offenses.heading: OFFENSE: DIVERSION OF CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE BY REGISTRANTS, DISPENSERS, AND CERTAIN OTHER PERSONS

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Fraud
offenses.summary: Prescription and controlled-substance fraud: obtaining or attempting to obtain a controlled substance by fraud, forgery, deception, or a fraudulent prescription; misusing a DEA number; forging prescription signatures; "doctor shopping" for medically unnecessary prescriptions (a-1); making or possessing tools to counterfeit drugs or delivering counterfeit substances (b); or delivering or possessing prescriptions or prescription forms without a valid medical purpose (c).
offenses.notes: Schedules (I-V) are different from penalty groups. Schedules are set by the commissioner; penalty groups set most possession and delivery penalties.

Fraud (Distributes as a Registrant or Dispenser: Fraudulent Prescription Schedule II)
Fraud (Distributes as a Registrant or Dispenser: Fraudulent Prescription Schedule III/IV/V)
Fraud (Distributes as a Registrant or Dispenser: Schedule I/II)
Fraud (Distributes as a Registrant or Dispenser: Schedule III/IV)
Fraud (Distributes as a Registrant or Dispenser: Schedule V)

Doctor shopping (a-1): any Schedule I or II substance
Doctor shopping (a-1): Schedule III or IV
Delivering a prescription form, or a Schedule II prescription, without a valid medical purpose (c)(1)
Delivering a Schedule III, IV, or V prescription (c)(1)

Possessing a Schedule IV or V prescription unlawfully (c)(2)

offenses.summary: Knowingly or intentionally uses or possesses with intent to use a substance or device designed to falsify drug test results (a); or delivers or makes one with intent to deliver (b).

offenses.heading: OFFENSE: FALSIFICATION OF DRUG TEST RESULTS

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Drug-Free Zones
offenses.summary: Not a separate offense. Raises drug offense levels when committed in a drug-free zone: within 1,000 feet of a school, school board property, youth center, or playground; on a school bus; within 300 feet of a public pool or video arcade (delivery only); near a college (delivery only); or by an adult within 1,000 feet of a residential treatment center. Delivery offenses go up one degree (state jail to third, third to second, second to first). Possession of less than 1 gram (PG 1, 2), fewer than 20 abuse units (PG 1-A), more than 4 ounces to 5 pounds of marihuana, and similar state jail tiers become third degree felonies; PG 3 under 28 grams and 2-4 ounces of marihuana become state jail felonies; PG 4 under 28 grams and 2 ounces or less of marihuana become Class A misdemeanors.
offenses.heading: DRUG-FREE ZONES

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Unlawful Transfer or Receipt of Chemical Precursor
offenses.summary: Sells, transfers, furnishes, or receives a regulated chemical precursor without complying with the reporting and record rules, or knowingly makes a false report or violates a related rule.

tiers.when: Prior conviction under this section or 481.137

offenses.heading: OFFENSE: UNLAWFUL TRANSFER OR RECEIPT OF CHEMICAL PRECURSOR

offenses.heading: OFFENSE: TRANSFER OF PRECURSOR SUBSTANCE FOR UNLAWFUL MANUFACTURE

offenses.heading: OFFENSE: TRANSFER OF CHEMICAL LABORATORY APPARATUS FOR UNLAWFUL MANUFACTURE

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes

offenses.summary: Not a separate offense. A state jail, third, or second degree drug manufacture or delivery offense is raised one degree if the defendant used or tried to use a child under 18 to commit or assist it, or becomes a first degree felony if force or threats were used to get the child's help. offenses.heading: USE OF CHILD IN COMMISSION OF OFFENSE

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Drug Manufacture or Delivery Causing Death or Serious Bodily Injury
offenses.summary: Not a separate offense. A state jail, third, or second degree drug manufacture or delivery offense is raised one degree if a person died or suffered serious bodily injury from taking the substance the defendant made or delivered. The sentence cannot run concurrently. Does not apply if the defendant is also prosecuted for murder under PC 19.02(b)(4) (fentanyl).
offenses.heading: MANUFACTURE OR DELIVERY OF CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE CAUSING DEATH OR SERIOUS BODILY INJURY

offenses.heading: UNLAWFUL DELIVERY OR MANUFACTURE WITH INTENT TO DELIVER; CRIMINAL PENALTY

offenses.notes: A "dangerous drug" is any drug or device labeled "Rx only" (or the federal prescription legend) that is not in Schedules I-V or Penalty Groups 1-4 (483.001).

offenses.name: Manufacture of Dangerous Drug

offenses.name: Failure to Maintain Records

offenses.name: Refusal to Permit Inspection

offenses.group: Subtitle C. Substance Abuse Regulation and Crimes
offenses.name: Violation of Other Provision

offenses.name: Prohibited Acts

offenses.name: Prohibited Use of Fireworks

offenses.notes: Each day is a separate offense. Counties and cities may further restrict or ban fireworks (for example during drought), and city ordinances often prohibit fireworks inside city limits; check local ordinances.

Each day is a separate offense.
offenses.heading: PENALTIES

offenses.group: Title 1. Introductory Provisions
offenses.name: Key Definitions
offenses.summary: Definitions used throughout the Penal Code. Bodily injury: physical pain, illness, or any impairment of physical condition. Serious bodily injury: injury creating a substantial risk of death, or causing death, serious permanent disfigurement, or protracted loss or impairment of a bodily member or organ. Deadly weapon: a firearm or anything designed or adapted to cause death or serious bodily injury, or anything that in its manner of use or intended use is capable of causing death or serious bodily injury. Public place: any place the public or a substantial group of the public can access, including streets, highways, and common areas of schools, hospitals, apartments, office buildings, transport facilities, and shops. Effective consent is not effective if induced by force, threat, or fraud; given by someone known not to be authorized; given by someone known to be unable to decide because of youth, mental defect, or intoxication; or given only to detect an offense. Possession: actual care, custody, control, or management.
offenses.heading: DEFINITIONS

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Culpable Mental States
offenses.summary: Intentionally: the person's conscious objective or desire is to engage in the conduct or cause the result. Knowingly: aware of the nature of the conduct or that the circumstances exist, or aware the conduct is reasonably certain to cause the result. Recklessly: aware of but consciously disregards a substantial and unjustifiable risk (a gross deviation from ordinary care). Criminal negligence: ought to be aware of a substantial and unjustifiable risk, and failing to perceive it is a gross deviation from ordinary care.
offenses.heading: DEFINITIONS OF CULPABLE MENTAL STATES

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.chapter: Ch. 7 Criminal Responsibility for Conduct of Another
offenses.name: Parties to an Offense (Criminal Responsibility for Conduct of Another)
offenses.summary: A person is criminally responsible for another's offense if, with the required culpability, they cause or aid an innocent person to commit it; or, intending to promote or assist it, they solicit, encourage, direct, aid, or attempt to aid the other; or, having a legal duty to prevent it, they fail to make a reasonable effort to prevent it. In a conspiracy to commit one felony, all conspirators are guilty of another felony committed in furtherance of it that should have been anticipated.
offenses.heading: CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR CONDUCT OF ANOTHER

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.chapter: Ch. 8 General Defenses to Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Intoxication (Not a Defense)
offenses.summary: Voluntary intoxication is not a defense to a crime. Temporary insanity caused by intoxication may be offered only to reduce the penalty.
offenses.heading: INTOXICATION

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.chapter: Ch. 8 General Defenses to Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Age Affecting Criminal Responsibility
offenses.summary: A person cannot be prosecuted as an adult for most offenses committed before age 17 unless the juvenile court certifies them. Under 15, prosecution is limited to fine-only misdemeanors, traffic offenses, city ordinance violations, perjury, and offenses transferred from juvenile court. Children younger than 10 cannot be prosecuted for fine-only offenses or ordinance violations, and children 10 to 14 are presumed incapable of them unless the state proves otherwise. No one may be sentenced to death for an offense committed under 18.
offenses.heading: AGE AFFECTING CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Necessity
offenses.summary: Conduct is justified if the actor reasonably believes it is immediately necessary to avoid imminent harm, the urgency of avoiding that harm clearly outweighs the harm the law seeks to prevent, and the Legislature has not plainly excluded the defense.
offenses.heading: NECESSITY

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Self-Defense
offenses.summary: Force is justified when and to the degree the actor reasonably believes it is immediately necessary to protect against another's use or attempted use of unlawful force. The belief is presumed reasonable if the other person was unlawfully and forcibly entering (or trying to enter) the actor's occupied home, vehicle, or workplace, or forcibly removing the actor from it, or was committing aggravated kidnapping, murder, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, robbery, or aggravated robbery, and the actor did not provoke it and was not engaged in criminal activity (other than a Class C traffic violation). Force is NOT justified in response to words alone, to resist an arrest or search the actor knows a peace officer is making (even if unlawful), if the actor consented or provoked the encounter (unless they withdrew), or while seeking a confrontation while unlawfully carrying a weapon. Resisting an arrest is justified only if the officer first uses greater force than necessary. No duty to retreat if lawfully present, not the provoker, and not engaged in crime.
offenses.heading: SELF-DEFENSE

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Deadly Force in Defense of Person
offenses.summary: Deadly force is justified if force would be justified under 9.31 and the actor reasonably believes deadly force is immediately necessary to protect against another's unlawful deadly force, or to prevent the imminent commission of aggravated kidnapping, murder, sexual assault, aggravated sexual assault, robbery, or aggravated robbery. The same presumption of reasonableness applies (unlawful forcible entry into an occupied home, vehicle, or workplace, etc.). No duty to retreat if lawfully present, not the provoker, and not engaged in criminal activity; failure to retreat may not be considered.
offenses.heading: DEADLY FORCE IN DEFENSE OF PERSON

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Defense of Third Person
offenses.summary: Force or deadly force is justified to protect another person if, as the actor reasonably believes the circumstances to be, the actor would be justified under 9.31 or 9.32 in protecting themselves from the threat facing that person, and reasonably believes intervening is immediately necessary.
offenses.heading: DEFENSE OF THIRD PERSON

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Protection of One's Own Property
offenses.summary: A person lawfully possessing land or movable property may use force reasonably believed immediately necessary to prevent or end another's trespass or unlawful interference. A person unlawfully dispossessed may use force to reenter or recover the property immediately or in fresh pursuit, if the other had no claim of right or used force, threat, or fraud.
offenses.heading: PROTECTION OF ONE'S OWN PROPERTY

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Deadly Force to Protect Property
offenses.summary: Deadly force to protect property is justified only if force is justified under 9.41, the actor reasonably believes deadly force is immediately necessary to prevent imminent arson, burglary, robbery, aggravated robbery, nighttime theft, or nighttime criminal mischief, or to stop someone fleeing with property immediately after burglary, robbery, aggravated robbery, or nighttime theft, AND the actor reasonably believes the property cannot be protected or recovered any other way, or that lesser force would expose someone to a substantial risk of death or serious bodily injury.
offenses.heading: DEADLY FORCE TO PROTECT PROPERTY

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Arrest and Search (Use of Force by Peace Officers)
offenses.summary: A peace officer (or person acting at an officer's direction) may use force reasonably believed immediately necessary to make or assist an arrest or search, or prevent escape after arrest, if the officer reasonably believes the arrest or search is lawful (or the warrant valid) and first identifies themselves and their purpose unless it is already known or cannot reasonably be made known. Deadly force is justified to make an arrest or prevent escape only if force is justified and the officer reasonably believes the conduct for the arrest included the use or attempted use of deadly force, or that there is a substantial risk the person will cause death or serious bodily injury to the officer or another if the arrest is delayed. Private persons have narrower authority.
offenses.heading: ARREST AND SEARCH

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Prevention of Escape From Custody
offenses.summary: Force to prevent an arrested person's escape is justified when it could have been used to make the arrest. A correctional guard or peace officer may use any force, including deadly force, reasonably believed immediately necessary to prevent an escape from a correctional facility.
offenses.heading: PREVENTION OF ESCAPE FROM CUSTODY

offenses.group: Title 2. General Principles of Criminal Responsibility
offenses.name: Parent-Child (Discipline)
offenses.summary: A parent, stepparent, or person acting in place of a parent (including a grandparent, guardian, or someone with the parent's consent) may use force, but not deadly force, against a child under 18 when and to the degree reasonably believed necessary to discipline the child or safeguard their welfare.
offenses.heading: PARENT-CHILD

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Classification of Misdemeanors
offenses.summary: Misdemeanors are Class A, B, or C. A misdemeanor with no stated punishment or class is a Class C misdemeanor. A Class C conviction imposes no legal disability.
offenses.heading: CLASSIFICATION OF MISDEMEANORS

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Classification of Felonies
offenses.summary: Felonies are capital, first, second, third degree, and state jail felonies. A felony with no stated category is a state jail felony.
offenses.heading: CLASSIFICATION OF FELONIES

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: State Jail Felony Punishment
offenses.summary: State jail felony: 180 days to 2 years in a state jail and a fine up to $10,000. It is punished as a third degree felony if a deadly weapon was used or exhibited (by the actor, or a party who knew one would be used), or if the person has a prior conviction for a "3g" offense listed in CCP Art. 42A.054(a) or continuous sexual abuse, or a prior judgment with a deadly weapon finding.
offenses.heading: STATE JAIL FELONY PUNISHMENT

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Classification of Offenses Outside This Code
offenses.summary: For enhancement, a conviction from outside the Penal Code counts as a third degree felony if it carried possible prison time, a Class B misdemeanor if it carried possible jail time, and a Class C misdemeanor if fine only.
offenses.heading: CLASSIFICATION OF OFFENSES OUTSIDE THIS CODE

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Repeat and Habitual Felony Offenders
offenses.summary: Raises felony punishment for prior felony convictions (not counting state jail felonies punished under 12.35(a)): a third degree felony is punished as second degree with one prior felony; second degree as first degree; first degree becomes 15 to 99 years or life. With two sequential prior felonies (habitual offender), any first, second, or third degree felony becomes 25 to 99 years or life. Repeat sex offenders face mandatory life, and in some cases a capital felony.
offenses.heading: PENALTIES FOR REPEAT AND HABITUAL FELONY OFFENDERS ON TRIAL FOR FIRST, SECOND, OR THIRD DEGREE FELONY

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Repeat and Habitual Offenders on Trial for State Jail Felony
offenses.summary: A state jail felony is punished as third degree with two prior state jail felonies; as second degree with two sequential prior non-state-jail felonies; and as second degree when it is already enhanced under 12.35(c) (deadly weapon or listed prior) and there is a prior non-state-jail felony.
offenses.heading: PENALTIES FOR REPEAT AND HABITUAL FELONY OFFENDERS ON TRIAL FOR STATE JAIL FELONY

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Repeat and Habitual Misdemeanor Offenders
offenses.summary: A Class A misdemeanor with a prior Class A or felony conviction: 90 days to 1 year minimum range. A Class B with a prior Class A, Class B, or felony: 30 to 180 days. Disorderly conduct or public intoxication (Class C) with three priors under either section within 24 months: punished as a Class B (up to 180 days and $2,000). A specific repeat-offender provision in the offense itself controls over this section.
offenses.heading: PENALTIES FOR REPEAT AND HABITUAL MISDEMEANOR OFFENDERS

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Reduction of State Jail Felony Punishment to Misdemeanor Punishment
offenses.summary: A court may punish a state jail felony with Class A misdemeanor confinement, and on the prosecutor's request may let the state prosecute a state jail felony as a Class A misdemeanor.
offenses.heading: REDUCTION OF STATE JAIL FELONY PUNISHMENT TO MISDEMEANOR PUNISHMENT

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Hate Crime Enhancement
offenses.summary: If the court finds the offense was committed because of bias or prejudice (CCP Art. 42.014), the punishment is raised to the next higher category (except a first degree felony), and a Class A misdemeanor gets a minimum of 180 days.
offenses.heading: PENALTY IF OFFENSE COMMITTED BECAUSE OF BIAS OR PREJUDICE

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Penalty If Controlled Substance Used to Commit Offense
offenses.summary: If the court finds a controlled substance was used to commit a robbery, theft, or Title 5 offense against the person (CCP Art. 42.012), the punishment is raised to the next higher category (except a first degree felony), and a Class A misdemeanor gets a minimum of 180 days.
offenses.heading: PENALTY IF CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE USED TO COMMIT OFFENSE

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Offense in Disaster Area or Evacuated Area
offenses.summary: Smuggling or stash house (20.05-20.07), assault, arson, robbery, burglary, burglary of a coin machine or vehicle, criminal trespass, theft, and interference with public duties are raised one category if committed in a declared disaster area or under an evacuation order. Class A misdemeanors get a minimum of 180 days; smuggling and stash house offenses get minimums of 10 or 15 years.
offenses.heading: PENALTY IF OFFENSE COMMITTED IN DISASTER AREA OR EVACUATED AREA

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Penalty for Certain Offenses Committed in Retaliation for or on Account of Person's Service or Status as Public Servant
offenses.summary: Listed offenses (including intimate visual material, sexual coercion, sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief, trespass, computer breach, harassment, and stalking) are raised one category if committed against a public servant, their family or household, or their property, in retaliation for their service.
offenses.heading: PENALTY FOR CERTAIN OFFENSES COMMITTED IN RETALIATION FOR OR ON ACCOUNT OF PERSON'S SERVICE OR STATUS AS PUBLIC SERVANT

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Penalty If Offense Committed on Premises of Postsecondary Educational Institution
offenses.summary: Public lewdness, indecent exposure, and invasive visual recording committed on the premises of a college, university, or career school are raised one category.
offenses.heading: PENALTY IF OFFENSE COMMITTED ON PREMISES OF POSTSECONDARY EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTION

offenses.group: Title 3. Punishments
offenses.name: Penalty If Metal or Body Armor Used During Commission of Offense
offenses.summary: If the court finds the defendant wore metal or body armor during the offense (CCP Art. 42.01992), the punishment is raised to the next higher category.
offenses.heading: PENALTY IF METAL OR BODY ARMOR USED DURING COMMISSION OF OFFENSE

offenses.group: Title 5. Offenses Against the Person
offenses.name: Terroristic Threat
offenses.summary: Threatens to commit any offense involving violence to any person or property, with intent to cause an emergency response, place someone in fear of imminent serious bodily injury, disrupt a building or public place, interrupt public services, put the public in fear, or influence government.

tiers.when: Intent to cause a reaction by an emergency agency (a)(1)
Intent to place a person in fear of imminent serious bodily injury (a)(2)
Fear of serious bodily injury, against family or household or constituting family violence
Fear of serious bodily injury, against a public servant
Fear of serious bodily injury, against a person the actor knows is a peace officer or judge
Intent to prevent or interrupt use of a building or public place (a)(3)
Interrupting a building or public place, causing pecuniary loss of $1,500 or more
Intent to impair public services, place the public in fear of serious bodily injury, or influence government (a)(4)-(6)

offenses.heading: TERRORISTIC THREAT

offenses.group: Title 5. Offenses Against the Person
offenses.name: Aiding Suicide
