cases.facts: Officers saw a man put a bag they believed held marijuana into his trunk, then stopped the car and opened the bag.
cases.held: Under the automobile exception, officers may search a container in a vehicle when they have probable cause to believe it holds contraband, without a warrant.
cases.patrol: Probable cause defines the scope: wherever the item could be found.

cases.name: Wyoming v. Houghton
cases.facts: With probable cause to search a car for drugs, an officer searched a passenger's purse on the back seat.
cases.held: Officers with probable cause to search a car may inspect passengers' belongings in the car that could hold the object of the search.
cases.patrol: Probable cause for the car extends to passenger containers capable of holding the item.

cases.name: Arizona v. Gant
cases.facts: A driver was arrested for driving with a suspended license, handcuffed, and locked in a patrol car; officers then searched his car and found cocaine.
cases.held: Officers may search a vehicle incident to a recent occupant's arrest only if (1) the arrestee is unsecured and within reaching distance of the passenger compartment, or (2) it is reasonable to believe evidence of the offense of arrest is in the vehicle.
cases.patrol: No automatic car search after arrest. A DWI or drug arrest may support an evidence search; a license or warrant arrest usually does not. Use probable cause or inventory instead.

cases.name: South Dakota v. Opperman
cases.facts: A car impounded for parking violations was inventoried under standard procedure, and marijuana was found in the glove box.
cases.held: A routine inventory of a lawfully impounded vehicle, under standard police procedure, is reasonable without a warrant.
cases.patrol: The impound must be lawful and the inventory must follow your written policy.

cases.name: Colorado v. Bertine
cases.facts: After a DUI arrest, officers inventoried the van and opened a closed backpack, finding drugs and cash.
cases.held: Inventory searches of closed containers are valid if done under standardized criteria and not in bad faith or solely to investigate.
cases.patrol: Follow the policy every time. An inventory that is really an evidence search will be suppressed.

cases.name: Collins v. Virginia
cases.facts: An officer walked up a driveway to a partially enclosed area next to a house and lifted a tarp to look at a motorcycle.
cases.held: The automobile exception does not allow an officer to enter a home or its curtilage without a warrant to search a vehicle parked there.
cases.patrol: A car parked in an enclosed driveway or carport next to the house is protected like the house. Get a warrant.

cases.name: Schneckloth v. Bustamonte
cases.facts: After a traffic stop, an officer asked to search the car; the person in control said "Sure, go ahead."
cases.held: Consent is valid if voluntary under the totality of the circumstances. The officer need not tell the person they may refuse, though knowledge of the right to refuse is a factor.
cases.patrol: Telling the person they can refuse is not required, but it strengthens the consent. Texas requires the State to prove voluntariness by clear and convincing evidence.

cases.name: Florida v. Jimeno
cases.facts: A driver consented to a search of his car for narcotics; the officer opened a folded paper bag on the floorboard.
cases.held: The scope of consent is what a reasonable person would have understood from the exchange. Consent to search a car for drugs includes closed containers that could hold drugs.
cases.patrol: State the object of the search when asking ("Can I search the car for drugs?"). The person may limit or withdraw consent.

cases.name: Illinois v. Rodriguez
cases.facts: A woman let officers into an apartment she called "our" apartment; she had in fact moved out.
cases.held: A search is valid if officers reasonably (even if mistakenly) believe the consenting person has authority over the premises (apparent authority).
cases.patrol: Ask questions to confirm the person lives there or controls the area.

cases.name: Georgia v. Randolph
cases.facts: A wife consented to a search of the home while her husband, standing at the door, expressly refused.
cases.held: A physically present co-occupant's express refusal overrides another occupant's consent to search a shared home.
cases.patrol: If the other resident is there and says no, you need a warrant or an exception.

cases.name: Payton v. New York
cases.facts: Officers with probable cause, but no warrant, forced entry into a home to make a routine felony arrest.
cases.held: Absent consent or exigent circumstances, officers may not enter a home to make a routine arrest without a warrant.
cases.patrol: Same rule in Texas: CCP 14.05 bars entering a residence for a warrantless arrest without consent or exigent circumstances.

cases.name: Brigham City v. Stuart
cases.facts: Officers responding to a loud party at 3 a.m. saw through a window a juvenile punch an adult, drawing blood, and entered.
cases.held: Officers may enter a home without a warrant when they have an objectively reasonable basis for believing an occupant is seriously injured or imminently threatened with such injury.
cases.patrol: The emergency-aid exception. Document what you saw or heard that made the emergency reasonable to believe.

cases.name: Case v. Montana
cases.facts: Officers entered a suicidal man's home without a warrant to check on him after he had threatened to shoot himself.
cases.held: Brigham City's objective-reasonableness standard governs emergency-aid entries, with no added requirement of probable cause. It was met here.
cases.patrol: For welfare emergencies you need an objectively reasonable belief someone inside needs immediate help, not probable cause of a crime.

cases.name: Kentucky v. King
cases.facts: Officers smelled marijuana at an apartment door, knocked loudly, announced themselves, heard movement suggesting evidence was being destroyed, and entered.
cases.held: The exigency rule applies when police do not create the exigency by engaging or threatening to engage in conduct that violates the Fourth Amendment. Knocking and announcing is lawful conduct.
cases.patrol: You may knock like any citizen. Do not threaten entry you have no right to make. Texas applies this to destruction-of-evidence claims strictly (see Turrubiate).

cases.name: Lange v. California
cases.facts: An officer followed a driver who was playing loud music and honking, signaled him to stop, and followed him into his garage when he did not.
cases.held: Pursuit of a fleeing misdemeanor suspect does not always justify a warrantless home entry. Officers must evaluate case by case whether a true emergency exists (for example, imminent harm, destruction of evidence, or escape).
cases.patrol: Felony hot pursuit generally allows entry. For misdemeanors, articulate a specific exigency beyond the flight itself.

cases.name: Caniglia v. Strom
cases.facts: After a man put a handgun on the table during an argument, officers took him for a psychiatric evaluation and entered his home to seize his guns.
cases.held: "Community caretaking" is not a freestanding exception that allows warrantless searches and seizures in the home.
cases.patrol: Home entries need a warrant, consent, or a real exigency such as emergency aid.

cases.name: Maryland v. Buie
cases.facts: Officers arresting a robbery suspect at home looked into the basement and saw a red running suit used in the robbery.
cases.held: Incident to an in-home arrest, officers may look in spaces immediately adjoining the place of arrest from which an attack could launch. A broader protective sweep requires reasonable suspicion that someone dangerous is there, and it must be a quick look where a person could hide.
cases.patrol: A sweep is for people, not evidence.

cases.name: Florida v. Jardines
cases.facts: Officers brought a drug dog onto a home's front porch, where it alerted.
cases.held: Using a drug dog on a home's porch to investigate is a search; it exceeds the implied license to approach and knock.
cases.patrol: A knock-and-talk is fine. Bringing a K-9 to the door is not, without a warrant.

cases.name: Chimel v. California
cases.facts: Officers arrested a man at home on a warrant and then searched the entire house.
cases.held: A search incident to arrest is limited to the arrestee's person and the area within their immediate control (where they could reach a weapon or destroy evidence).
cases.patrol: Arrest does not open the whole house.

cases.name: Atwater v. City of Lago Vista
cases.facts: A Lago Vista, Texas officer arrested a mother for seatbelt violations, a fine-only offense.
cases.held: The Fourth Amendment allows a warrantless custodial arrest for a minor, fine-only offense committed in the officer's presence.
cases.patrol: Texas law narrows this: Transportation Code 543.004 requires a written notice to appear (not arrest) for speeding, open container, and texting while driving when the person signs the promise to appear, and CCP 14.06 governs cite-and-release. Check department policy.

cases.name: Horton v. California
cases.facts: Officers executing a warrant for stolen jewelry saw guns used in the robbery, which were not listed in the warrant, and seized them.
cases.held: Plain view seizure is valid if the officer is lawfully in the place, the item's incriminating character is immediately apparent, and the officer has lawful access to it. Discovery need not be inadvertent.
cases.patrol: You must be lawfully where you are, and probable cause must be immediately apparent without moving things.

cases.name: Miranda v. Arizona
cases.facts: Suspects were questioned in custody without being told of their rights and confessed.
cases.held: Before custodial interrogation, a suspect must be warned of the right to remain silent, that statements can be used against them, the right to an attorney, and the right to an appointed attorney. Statements obtained without the warnings and a valid waiver are inadmissible.
cases.patrol: Custody plus interrogation equals warnings. In Texas, CCP 38.22 also requires the right to terminate the interview and a recording for oral statements.

cases.name: Berkemer v. McCarty
cases.facts: A driver stopped for weaving was questioned at roadside about drinking, then arrested for DUI and questioned more.
cases.held: Miranda applies to custodial interrogation for any offense, even misdemeanor traffic. Ordinary roadside questioning during a traffic stop is not custody. Once a person is under arrest or treated as if under arrest, warnings are required.
cases.patrol: Roadside DWI questions are usually fine. Post-arrest questioning needs warnings.

cases.name: Edwards v. Arizona
cases.facts: A suspect asked for a lawyer; officers returned the next day and got a confession.
cases.held: Once a suspect invokes the right to counsel, police may not interrogate again until counsel is present, unless the suspect starts further communication.
cases.patrol: When they ask for a lawyer, stop questioning. Document it if they reinitiate.

cases.name: Rhode Island v. Innis
cases.facts: Officers talked to each other in the patrol car about the danger of a missing shotgun near a school for disabled children; the suspect then led them to it.
cases.held: "Interrogation" includes express questioning and any words or actions police should know are reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response. This conversation did not qualify.
cases.patrol: Do not use staged conversations to get around Miranda.

cases.name: New York v. Quarles
cases.facts: An officer cornered a rape suspect in a supermarket, found an empty holster, and asked where the gun was before giving warnings.
cases.held: A public safety exception allows questions reasonably prompted by an immediate concern for public safety before Miranda warnings.
cases.patrol: Limit unwarned questions to the immediate danger ("Where is the gun?"), then warn.

cases.name: Berghuis v. Thompkins
cases.facts: A warned suspect stayed mostly silent for almost three hours, then answered "yes" when asked if he prayed for forgiveness for the shooting.
cases.held: A suspect must invoke the right to remain silent unambiguously. A knowing and voluntary statement after warnings can be an implied waiver.
cases.patrol: Ambiguous statements do not require you to stop, but Texas courts look closely at the recording. Clarify if unsure.

cases.name: Pennsylvania v. Muniz
cases.facts: A DUI arrestee was videotaped answering booking questions and performing sobriety tests, and was asked the date of his sixth birthday.
cases.held: Slurred speech and sobriety-test performance are physical, not testimonial, evidence. Routine booking questions (name, address, height, weight, date of birth, age) fall within an exception. The sixth-birthday question was testimonial and needed warnings.
cases.patrol: SFSTs and booking questions are fine without Miranda; do not ask questions designed to test mental processing in custody without warnings.

cases.name: Missouri v. McNeely
cases.facts: A DWI suspect who refused a breath test had blood drawn without a warrant in a routine case.
cases.held: The natural dissipation of alcohol does not create a per se exigency. Whether a warrantless blood draw is justified by exigency is decided case by case on the totality of the circumstances.
cases.patrol: Get a blood warrant. Exigency must be shown with specific facts (see Cole).

cases.name: Birchfield v. North Dakota
cases.facts: Three drivers challenged state laws making it a crime to refuse breath or blood tests after a DUI arrest.
cases.held: A breath test is allowed as a search incident to a lawful drunk-driving arrest without a warrant. A blood test is not; it needs a warrant, consent, or exigency. States may not make it a crime to refuse a blood test.
cases.patrol: Breath is a search incident to arrest; blood requires a warrant, actual consent, or exigency.

cases.name: Mitchell v. Wisconsin
cases.facts: A drunk-driving suspect became unconscious and was taken to a hospital, where blood was drawn without a warrant.
cases.held: Plurality opinion: when a driver is unconscious and must be taken to a hospital before a breath test can be done, exigency will almost always permit a warrantless blood test. The case was remanded for the defendant to show otherwise.
cases.patrol: This is a plurality opinion. In Texas, implied consent alone does not justify a draw from an unconscious driver (State v. Ruiz); seek a warrant when practical.
cases.note: Plurality opinion; no single rationale had five votes.

cases.name: Graham v. Connor
cases.facts: A diabetic man having an insulin reaction was forcibly detained by officers who thought he had shoplifted.
cases.held: Excessive force claims during an arrest or stop are judged under the Fourth Amendment's objective reasonableness standard, from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, considering the severity of the crime, whether the suspect poses an immediate threat, and whether they are actively resisting or fleeing.
cases.patrol: Articulate the Graham factors in every use-of-force report.

cases.name: Tennessee v. Garner
cases.facts: An officer shot an unarmed, fleeing teenage burglary suspect to prevent his escape.
cases.held: Deadly force may not be used to prevent the escape of a fleeing suspect unless the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer or others (and, where feasible, gives a warning).
cases.patrol: Flight alone never justifies deadly force. See also Penal Code 9.51.

cases.name: Scott v. Harris
cases.facts: A deputy ended a dangerous high-speed chase by bumping the fleeing car, which crashed and left the driver paralyzed. Dash-cam video showed the danger.
cases.held: An officer's attempt to end a dangerous high-speed chase that threatens innocent bystanders is reasonable even when it places the fleeing driver at risk of serious injury or death.
cases.patrol: Follow your pursuit policy; video evidence of the danger matters.

cases.name: Barnes v. Felix
cases.facts: During a Houston-area toll stop, a driver started to drive off while an officer stood on the door sill, and the officer fired. The Fifth Circuit looked only at the two seconds before the shot ("moment-of-threat" rule).
cases.held: Courts may not limit the excessive-force analysis to the moment of the threat. Reasonableness is judged on the totality of the circumstances, including events leading up to the use of force.
cases.patrol: Your actions before the use of force count. Document the whole encounter.

cases.name: Riley v. California
cases.facts: Officers searched the phones of arrestees incident to arrest and found gang-related evidence.
cases.held: Officers generally may not search the digital contents of a cell phone seized from an arrestee without a warrant.
cases.patrol: Secure the phone; get a warrant. Texas CCP 18.0215 says the same and lists narrow exceptions.

cases.name: Carpenter v. United States
cases.facts: Prosecutors got 127 days of a robbery suspect's historical cell-site location records from his carriers by court order, without a warrant.
cases.held: Acquiring historical cell-site location information is a search; the government generally needs a warrant.
cases.patrol: Phone location history requires a warrant, not just a subpoena or court order.

cases.name: Mapp v. Ohio
cases.facts: Officers forced their way into a home without a valid warrant and found obscene materials.
cases.held: Evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment is inadmissible in state criminal trials (the exclusionary rule).
cases.patrol: Texas has its own, broader exclusionary rule in CCP 38.23.

cases.name: Utah v. Strieff
cases.facts: An officer stopped a man leaving a suspected drug house without enough suspicion, found he had an outstanding warrant, arrested him, and found drugs.
cases.held: Discovering a valid, pre-existing, untainted arrest warrant attenuated the connection between the unlawful stop and the evidence, so the evidence was admissible.
cases.patrol: Not a license for bad stops; flagrant or purposeful misconduct defeats attenuation.

cases.name: Franks v. Delaware
cases.facts: A defendant claimed the officer's search warrant affidavit contained false statements.
cases.held: If a defendant shows the affiant knowingly, intentionally, or with reckless disregard for the truth included a false statement needed for probable cause, the warrant is voided and the evidence suppressed.
cases.patrol: Every statement in your affidavit must be true and sourced.

cases.name: Brady v. Maryland
cases.facts: The prosecution withheld a co-defendant's confession to the killing.
cases.held: Suppressing evidence favorable to the accused that is material to guilt or punishment violates due process, regardless of good faith.
cases.patrol: Put everything in the report and case file, including evidence that helps the defense. Texas also requires broad disclosure (CCP 39.14).

cases.name: Crain v. State
cases.facts: Late at night, an officer shined his patrol car's light toward a man walking and said "come over here and talk to me."
cases.held: The light combined with a request that sounded like an order turned the interaction into a detention, and the officer lacked reasonable suspicion.
cases.patrol: Word choice matters. "Come over here" can be a command; "Can I talk to you?" is a request.

cases.name: State v. Garcia-Cantu
cases.facts: Before dawn, an officer parked behind a truck on a dead-end street, shined a spotlight on it, and approached.
cases.held: Under the totality of the circumstances, including blocking the truck and the spotlight, a reasonable person would not have felt free to leave, so the encounter was a detention requiring reasonable suspicion.
cases.patrol: Blocking a car in and lighting it up can make a "welfare check" a detention.

cases.name: Derichsweiler v. State
cases.facts: A driver repeatedly pulled alongside other cars at a fast-food restaurant and a store parking lot, staring and grinning at the occupants, and a witness called 911.
cases.held: Reasonable suspicion does not require that the officer identify a particular offense; it is enough that the facts reasonably suggest some criminal activity is afoot.
cases.patrol: Articulate why the behavior suggested crime, even if you cannot name the exact offense yet.

cases.name: State v. Kerwick
cases.facts: Responding to a fight call at a bar after midnight, an officer spoke with a man whose car was damaged; he pointed at a car across the street saying "there they are." The officer stopped it as it pulled away and found an intoxicated driver.
cases.held: Viewed in their totality, the facts gave reasonable suspicion for the stop. Courts must consider a witness's statement in context with everything else the officer knew, not take a piecemeal "divide-and-conquer" approach.
cases.patrol: Record what witnesses said and pointed out, and the context around it; get the witness's name.

cases.name: Kothe v. State
cases.facts: A deputy detained a driver for suspected DWI, found he was not intoxicated, but held him a few more minutes while a license and warrant check finished.
cases.held: A short continued detention to complete a routine license and warrant check was reasonable, even after the original suspicion was resolved.
cases.patrol: You may finish routine checks, but a stop must end once its purpose is done (see also Rodriguez).

cases.name: Lerma v. State
cases.facts: During a nighttime traffic stop, a passenger with no ID was nervous, kept trying to reach into his pockets, and moved his hands between the seats. The officer frisked him; he fled and was found with cocaine.
cases.held: The frisk was supported by reasonable suspicion that the passenger was armed and dangerous, and the stop was not unduly prolonged by the officer's questions of the passenger.
cases.patrol: Furtive movements and reaching toward hidden areas support a frisk. Keep questions within the stop's timeline.

cases.name: Furr v. State
cases.facts: Responding to an anonymous tip of drug use on a corner in a high-crime area, officers saw a man matching the description who walked away, kept looking back, sweated, and acted evasive.
cases.held: The tip corroborated by officers' own observations gave reasonable suspicion to detain, and the circumstances justified a frisk for safety.
cases.patrol: Corroborate the tip with your own observations (compare Florida v. J.L.).

cases.name: Lothrop v. State
cases.facts: A driver used an improved shoulder to pass a car that slowed at a railroad crossing.
cases.held: Driving on an improved shoulder is not an offense when it is necessary for one of the purposes listed in Transportation Code 545.058(a) and can be done safely. The officer had no reasonable suspicion because the driver's use fit the passing exception.
cases.patrol: For a shoulder stop, articulate why the use was not for an allowed purpose or was unsafe.

cases.name: Leming v. State
cases.facts: A caller reported a swerving driver; the officer saw the car weave and drift but the video did not clearly show it crossing the lane line.
cases.held: Even if the lane violation was unclear, the erratic driving gave reasonable suspicion to investigate whether the driver was intoxicated or impaired.
cases.patrol: Erratic driving can justify a DWI investigation stop even without a clear traffic violation. Note that the opinion's reading of "failure to maintain a single lane" (Part II) was a plurality.
cases.note: Part II (whether failing to maintain a lane is an offense without danger) did not have a majority.

cases.name: Jaganathan v. State
cases.facts: A driver passed a "Left Lane for Passing Only" sign and stayed in the left lane without passing.
cases.held: The trooper had reasonable suspicion of a violation; the facts did not show the driver needed to stay in the left lane for safety.
cases.patrol: Note that the driver passed the sign and was not passing or avoiding a hazard.

cases.name: Abney v. State
cases.facts: An officer stopped a car for driving in the left lane without passing, but did not testify that the driver had passed a "left lane for passing only" sign.
cases.held: Without specific facts that the driver passed the sign or otherwise violated the law, there was no reasonable suspicion.
cases.patrol: Your testimony must cover every element of the violation, such as the sign being posted and passed.

cases.name: Mahaffey v. State
cases.facts: A driver merged left without signaling where his lane ended and a sign said "Lane Ends, Merge Left."
cases.held: Merging when a lane ends is not a turn or lane change that requires a signal under the Transportation Code, so there was no violation.
cases.patrol: No signal stop for a forced merge where the lane ends.

cases.name: Keehn v. State
cases.facts: Officers saw a propane tank of anhydrous ammonia in a van parked in a driveway and entered the van to seize it.
cases.held: Under the automobile exception, a warrantless search of a readily mobile vehicle with probable cause is allowed without separate exigency; plain view alone does not authorize entry.
cases.patrol: Probable cause is the key. Plain view lets you see, not enter.
cases.note: Collins v. Virginia (2018) later held the automobile exception does not allow entering a home's curtilage to search a vehicle. Driveway cases need care.

cases.name: Turrubiate v. State
cases.facts: Deputies smelled marijuana at a home's door, made their presence known, and entered without a warrant.
cases.held: Probable cause that drugs are inside, the odor of marijuana, and officers making their presence known do not by themselves create exigent circumstances for a warrantless entry. There must be evidence that destruction of evidence was imminent.
cases.patrol: Odor at the door is a reason to get a warrant, not to go in.

cases.name: State v. Villarreal
cases.facts: A DWI suspect with prior convictions refused a specimen, and blood was drawn without a warrant under the mandatory-blood-draw statute.
cases.held: A warrantless, nonconsensual blood draw under the implied-consent and mandatory-blood-draw statutes is not a recognized exception to the warrant requirement and violated the Fourth Amendment. Implied consent that cannot be withdrawn is not valid consent.
cases.patrol: The mandatory blood statute does not replace a warrant. Get a warrant or show real exigency.

cases.name: Cole v. State
cases.facts: A driver crashed at about 110 mph into another car at an intersection, killing the other driver; the scene required many officers for hours.
cases.held: The record showed obtaining a warrant was impractical, so the warrantless blood draw was justified by exigent circumstances.
cases.patrol: If you rely on exigency, document why a warrant was not practical: scene demands, officers available, time to a judge, alcohol dissipation.

cases.name: State v. Ruiz
cases.facts: An unconscious driver after a crash had blood drawn at a hospital without a warrant based on implied consent.
cases.held: Irrevocable implied consent is not free and voluntary and does not satisfy the consent exception for an unconscious driver. The exigency question was sent back for reconsideration under Mitchell v. Wisconsin.
cases.patrol: For unconscious drivers, get a warrant or document exigency; do not rely on implied consent.

cases.name: State v. Martinez
cases.facts: After a fatal crash, a hospital drew blood for treatment; a trooper later took the vials without a warrant and had them tested.
cases.held: A person has a Fourth Amendment privacy interest in blood drawn for medical purposes. The State's testing of that blood is a search requiring a warrant (records may be obtained by subpoena).
cases.patrol: For hospital blood, get a warrant before the State tests it.

cases.name: Fienen v. State
cases.facts: A DWI arrestee who first refused asked the trooper many questions about a blood warrant and his options, then agreed to a breath test.
cases.held: Voluntariness of consent to a breath or blood test is judged on the totality of the circumstances. The court overruled Erdman v. State, so statements beyond the DIC-24 warnings are not automatically coercive. Consent here was voluntary.
cases.patrol: Read the DIC-24 exactly and answer questions truthfully. Do not threaten or promise consequences not in the statute.

cases.name: State v. Granville
cases.facts: A student arrested for a Class C offense had his phone stored in the jail property room; another officer retrieved it and searched it without a warrant.
cases.held: A person keeps a legitimate expectation of privacy in the contents of a cell phone while it is stored in a jail property room.
cases.patrol: A phone in property still needs a warrant.

cases.name: Holder v. State
cases.facts: In a murder case, the State got 23 days of the suspect's historical cell-site location data with a court order rather than a warrant.
cases.held: Under the Texas Constitution (Art. I, Sec. 9), the person had a reasonable expectation of privacy in that location data, and the third-party doctrine alone did not defeat it.
cases.patrol: In Texas, location history needs a warrant under both the state and federal constitutions.

cases.name: Wehrenberg v. State
cases.facts: Officers entered an apartment without a warrant while waiting for one; the warrant was later issued based on information they had before the entry.
cases.held: The federal independent source doctrine applies in Texas: evidence later obtained through a source independent of the illegal entry is not "obtained" in violation of law under CCP 38.23.
cases.patrol: This is a safety net, not a plan. Do not enter while waiting for a warrant.

common.source: Texas DPS arrest statistics, calendar year 2025
